p: The manuscripts tell the parable of the two sons in three different ways. This entry goes with 21:30 and 21:31.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (03), Θ, family 13, 700, Armenian and some Syriac (as reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort
readings.en: I will, sir; and he did not go

why: In the second form the order of the sons is reversed and the answer becomes "the last" (21:31). The form followed is the one with the widest support. The order "no, then yes" first may have been changed so that the obedient son (taken as the Gentiles or sinners who came later) comes second.
b: A third form, in Bezae (05) and some Old Latin and Syriac copies, has the first son refuse and go, yet the leaders answer "the last." Many think this makes the leaders give a perverse answer on purpose; Metzger called it nonsensical as it stands, though Jerome knew it and explained it as the leaders' stubbornness.

why: The verse is missing from the earliest manuscripts of every major type. Where it does appear, it stands in different places: before 23:13 in most later copies, after it in a few. A saying that floats like that was most likely added from the parallels in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47, where it is original.
b: The KJV prints it after 23:13 and numbers it 23:14 (printed Greek editions of the Textus Receptus differ on where they place it), and so the verse number is kept here with a note, as in most modern Bibles. The Byzantine Textform prints the widows' woe as 23:13 and the woe about shutting the kingdom as 23:14. The saying itself is genuine teaching of Jesus in Mark and Luke: it charges some teachers with taking advantage of widows, perhaps as trustees of their property, while making a show of piety.

why: The words are in nearly every witness, and the shorter text is most easily explained as a correction: a copyist who knew that the Zechariah killed in the temple was the son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20–22) may have removed the problem. Jerome reports that the gospel used by the Nazarenes, Jewish Christians, read "son of Jehoiada" instead. Luke 11:51 has no father's name.

p: Codex Vaticanus and a few others lack "deserted"; most manuscripts have it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (03), L, some Old Latin, the Sinaitic Syriac (as reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort

why: "Deserted" has broad support. It may have been added from Jeremiah 22:5, or dropped to match Luke 13:35, which lacks it; Metzger's committee kept it. Without it the sentence means "your house is left to you," that is, God leaves it.
